literature.headline_zh: 沙粒病毒科本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期沙粒病毒科研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 研究发现,SSP 经历了两种不同的结构变化:第一个在 pH 6 时与融合无关,第二个在 pH 5 以下与融合活性相关。此外,K33A 突变 至 SSP 不会发生这两种结构变化,而是在 pH 6 时发生不同的构象变化。 [10.1021/acs.biochem.6c00428]
研究结果表明,LCMV P52 优先在肿瘤中复制,表现出改善的肿瘤渗透性,更有效地吸引功能性 CD8+ T 细胞,并将肿瘤微环境重新编程为更具免疫原性。 [10.3390/v18090998]
主要结果表明,CEN抑制剂有效抑制病毒复制,并为拉沙热和阿根廷出血热豚鼠模型提供治疗保护。此外,该研究还确定了几种具有 抗病毒药物 活性的 CENis 对抗其他高致病性 沙粒病毒。 [10.1128/mbio.00880-26]
屠宰场,由于有机废物丰富和卫生条件差,为像Mastomys natalensis这样的啮齿动物提供了理想的生活条件,使其能够繁衍并污染表面和肉类产品。屠宰场工人由于常规且未受保护的接触动物组织、血液和生物气溶胶而面临严重的、未被充分认识的职业健康风险。受感染的工人作为入口点,可能会无意中成为媒介,将病毒引入家庭和社区,促进暴发。 [10.37432/jieph-d-25-00317]
本研究证明了LCMV恢复的小鼠表现出一种持续的免疫功能受损状态,主要影响新发T细胞反应,这种现象与脾脏淋巴组织的大规模破坏有关,影响了器官的分隔以及对有效T细胞激活至关重要的关键细胞-细胞接触。 [10.1038/s41419-026-09253-4]

literature.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
key_findings_en: The study found that SSP undergoes two distinct structural changes; the first at pH 6 that is not associated with fusion, and the second at below pH 5 that is associated with fusion activity. [10.1021/acs.biochem.6c00428]

The findings showed that LCMV P52 replicates preferentially in tumors, exhibits improved tumor penetration, attracts functional CD8+ T cells more effectively, and reprograms the tumor microenvironment to be more immunogenic. [10.3390/v18090998]

The main results showed that CEN inhibitors effectively suppressed viral replication and provided therapeutic protection in guinea pig models of Lassa fever and Argentine hemorrhagic fever. Additionally, the study identified several CENis with antiviral activity against other highly pathogenic arenaviruses. [10.1128/mbio.00880-26]

Abattoirs, characterized by abundant organic waste and inadequate sanitation, offer ideal conditions for rodents like Mastomys natalensis to thrive and contaminate surfaces and meat products. [10.37432/jieph-d-25-00317]

The study demonstrated that LCMV-recovered animals exhibit a prolonged immunocompromised state affecting dominantly de novo T cell responses, linked to the massive destruction of splenic lymphatic tissue, affecting the compartmentalization of the organ as well as crucial cell–cell contacts necessary for efficient T cell priming. [10.1038/s41419-026-09253-4]

key_findings_zh: 疾病预防控制中心及其全球健康安全专家正处于最前线,阻止致命威胁在美国蔓延。 [news-9d07b1160835f3c1]
奥约州报告131例疑似拉沙热病例,6例确诊,1例死亡。 [news-61f7ae36f74041bd]
奥约州政府报告了五例拉沙热的确诊病例和一例死亡,同时指出百日咳暴发导致两人死亡。卫生专员奥卢塞里米·阿杰图姆博博士警告医护人员要保持警惕,并概述了加强监测和应对措施。 [news-78827f8914a6c6df]
According to NCDC data, five states currently account for 86 percent of all reported cases in 2026: Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo, and Benue. [news-676773860cfe85d3]
尼日利亚疾病控制和预防中心(NCDC)敦促尼日利亚人采取预防措施,例如安全储存食物和封锁啮齿动物进入点,以在旺季到来之前减轻 拉沙热 的影响。这是经过确认的公共卫生建议,而不是 暴发 报告。 [news-c6b54d55ff74fd39]

news.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following Arenaviridae news developments.
key_findings_en: CDC and its global health security experts are on the frontlines stopping deadly threats before they can spread in the U.S. [news-9d07b1160835f3c1]
Oyo State reports 131 suspected Lassa fever cases, 6 confirmed, 1 death. [news-61f7ae36f74041bd]

Oyo State Government reported five confirmed cases and one death from Lassa fever, while also noting a diphtheria outbreak that claimed two lives. The Commissioner for Health, Dr Oluwaserimi Ajetunmobi, warned healthcare workers to maintain caution and outlined measures to strengthen surveillance and response. [news-78827f8914a6c6df]
According to NCDC data, five states currently account for 86 percent of all reported cases in 2026: Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo, and Benue. [news-676773860cfe85d3]

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) urged Nigerians to take preventive measures such as storing food safely and blocking rodent entry points to mitigate Lassa fever transmission ahead of the peak season. This is a confirmed public health advisory, not an outbreak report. [news-c6b54d55ff74fd39]

papers.title: Abattoirs as sentinel sites for Lassa fever surveillance: A One Health perspective in West Africa
papers.abstract: Lassa fever (LF), an acute viral haemorrhagic disease caused by Lassa virus (LASV), remains a significant public health concern in West Africa. The multimammate rat (Mastomys natalensis) is the principal reservoir, with humans primarily exposed through contact with infected rodent excreta and contaminated materials. Although healthcare workers are widely recognized as an occupationally vulnerable group, abattoir workers may represent an under-recognized population at risk because of frequent contact with animal blood and tissues, compounded by poor sanitation, inadequate rodent control, and inconsistent use of personal protective equipment (PPE). This review synthesizes available evidence on the occupational risk of Lassa virus exposure among abattoir workers and examines the broader public health implications, with emphasis on strengthening surveillance, biosafety, and integrated One Health interventions within abattoir settings. This is a narrative review that consolidates existing findings and literature on the epidemiology of Lassa fever, its virology and transmission pathways, the link between abattoirs and zoonotic disease exposure, rodent activity and biosecurity in abattoirs, and public health implications. Abattoirs, characterized by abundant organic waste and inadequate sanitation, offer ideal conditions for rodents like Mastomys natalensis to thrive and contaminate surfaces and meat products. Abattoir workers face a severe, under-recognized occupational health hazard due to routine and unprotected exposure to animal tissues, blood, and bioaerosols. Infected workers, serving as an entry point, can inadvertently act as vectors, introducing the virus into households and communities, fueling outbreaks. Abattoirs represent critical sentinel sites for early detection, as they centralize large animal populations and waste streams, allowing for detection of spillover events earlier than hospital-based systems. Abattoirs represent important yet addressable points of Lassa fever risk. Recognizing their potential as sentinel sites and integrating coordinated One Health interventions could help policymakers detect and disrupt hidden Lassa virus transmission pathways, protect at-risk population.
papers.journal: Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health

papers.source_body_en: Lassa fever (LF), an acute viral haemorrhagic disease caused by Lassa virus (LASV), remains a significant public health concern in West Africa. The multimammate rat (Mastomys natalensis) is the principal reservoir, with humans primarily exposed through contact with infected rodent excreta and contaminated materials. Although healthcare workers are widely recognized as an occupationally vulnerable group, abattoir workers may represent an under-recognized population at risk because of frequent contact with animal blood and tissues, compounded by poor sanitation, inadequate rodent control, and inconsistent use of personal protective equipment (PPE). This review synthesizes available evidence on the occupational risk of Lassa virus exposure among abattoir workers and examines the broader public health implications, with emphasis on strengthening surveillance, biosafety, and integrated One Health interventions within abattoir settings. This is a narrative review that consolidates existing findings and literature on the epidemiology of Lassa fever, its virology and transmission pathways, the link between abattoirs and zoonotic disease exposure, rodent activity and biosecurity in abattoirs, and public health implications. Abattoirs, characterized by abundant organic waste and inadequate sanitation, offer ideal conditions for rodents like Mastomys natalensis to thrive and contaminate surfaces and meat products. Abattoir workers face a severe, under-recognized occupational health hazard due to routine and unprotected exposure to animal tissues, blood, and bioaerosols. Infected workers, serving as an entry point, can inadvertently act as vectors, introducing the virus into households and communities, fueling outbreaks. Abattoirs represent critical sentinel sites for early detection, as they centralize large animal populations and waste streams, allowing for detection of spillover events earlier than hospital-based systems. Abattoirs represent important yet addressable points of Lassa fever risk. Recognizing their potential as sentinel sites and integrating coordinated One Health interventions could help policymakers detect and disrupt hidden Lassa virus transmission pathways, protect at-risk population.

papers.title: Lassa fever and Argentine hemorrhagic fever treatment in guinea pigs using broad-spectrum cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitors
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The class Bunyaviricetes encompasses several highly pathogenic viruses that cause lethal hemorrhagic fevers. Due to their limited prevention and treatment options and high pathogenicity, these viruses require handling in biosafety level-4 facilities. Within the bunyaviruses, arenaviruses are particularly notable for their pathogenicity and ability to cause severe hemorrhagic disease in humans. The cap-dependent endonuclease (CEN) is a unique and crucial enzyme involved in the replication cycle of these viruses. As humans do not possess a similar enzyme, CEN represents an ideal target for antiviral drug development with reduced risk of side effects. Recently, we identified a promising CEN inhibitor (CENi) demonstrating potent inhibition of virus replication. In this manuscript, we demonstrate the successful therapeutic efficacy of CENis against Lassa fever and Argentine hemorrhagic fever virus infections in guinea pig models of lethal hemorrhagic fever. In addition, we identified several CENis with antiviral activity against other highly pathogenic arenaviruses. These findings further support the potential of CENis as therapeutic agents for arenavirus infections that cause severe and often lethal hemorrhagic fever. Collectively, our results suggest that CENis are promising candidates for pan-arenavirus therapy and may also have broader utility against other CEN-containing viruses for which no approved antiviral treatments currently exist. IMPORTANCE Arenaviruses, such as Lassa virus and Junin virus, cause severe hemorrhagic fevers in humans and are associated with high mortality rates and limited treatment options. Because of their pathogenicity and potential for outbreaks, these viruses represent an important global health threat. The viral cap-dependent endonuclease (CEN) plays a critical role in arenavirus replication by enabling the cap-snatching process required for viral mRNA synthesis. Notably, mammalian cells lack a comparable enzyme, making CEN an attractive target for antiviral drug development. In this study, we demonstrate that inhibitors targeting the arenavirus CEN effectively suppress viral replication and provide therapeutic protection in animal models of lethal Lassa virus and Junin virus infections. We also identify compounds with antiviral activity against multiple highly pathogenic arenaviruses. These findings establish CEN inhibition as a promising strategy for the development of broad-spectrum antivirals against arenaviruses that cause life-threatening hemorrhagic fevers.

elements_zh.methods: 本研究利用CEN抑制剂来抑制病毒复制,并在拉沙热和阿根廷出血热的豚鼠模型中提供了治疗性保护。研究还鉴定了几种具有抗病毒药物活性的CENis,能够对抗多种高致病性沙粒病毒。
elements_zh.main_results: 主要结果表明,CEN抑制剂有效抑制病毒复制,并为拉沙热和阿根廷出血热豚鼠模型提供治疗保护。此外,该研究还确定了几种具有 抗病毒药物 活性的 CENis 对抗其他高致病性 沙粒病毒。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为支持 CEN 抑制剂作为 沙粒病毒 感染治疗药物的潜力,将 CEN 抑制确立为开发针对 沙粒病毒 的广谱 抗病毒药物 的有前途的策略。

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性包括使用动物模型以及需要进一步的临床试验来确认 CEN 抑制剂在人体中的功效。由于样本量有限且需要额外验证,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Biophysical Characterization of K33A Mutation to Stable Signal Peptide Reveals Insights into Lassa Virus Fusion Mechanism
papers.abstract: Abstract Lassa virus (LASV), a member of the arenavirus family, utilizes low-pH-dependent membrane fusion to enter host cells and elicit infection. LASV is a class I fusion virus, and thus its fusion protein, GP2, is functionally similar to other class I fusion proteins in that it follows the six-helix bundle fusion mechanism. LASV fusion is atypical in that it requires another viral protein, stable signal peptide (SSP), that does not undergo fusion itself but is required for the fusion process. However, the exact function of SSP in fusion is unknown. We aimed to understand the role of SSP in the fusion process by examining the structural changes that occur within SSP during the fusion process. We found that SSP undergoes two distinct structural changes; the first at pH 6 that is not associated with fusion, the second at below pH 5 that is associated with fusion activity. Furthermore, we found a mutation to a key residue of SSP, K33A, does not undergo these two structural changes; in fact, K33A is seen to undergo a different conformational change at pH 6. We believe this distinct conformation change is due to the loss of favorable interactions between the lysine at the end of the transmembrane helix of SSP. This disruption of favorable interaction then causes downstream effects to the SSP structure in the event of lowering pH. The difference in conformational changes between K33A and wildtype (WT) SSP is likely why K33A abrogates the fusion activity of GP2. We conclude that the conformational changes undergone by SSP are crucial for LASV fusion activity.

papers.title_zh: K33A 突变 稳定信号肽的生物物理表征揭示了对拉沙病毒融合机制的见解
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Lassa virus (LASV), a member of the arenavirus family, utilizes low-pH-dependent membrane fusion to enter host cells and elicit infection. LASV is a class I fusion virus, and thus its fusion protein, GP2, is functionally similar to other class I fusion proteins in that it follows the six-helix bundle fusion mechanism. LASV fusion is atypical in that it requires another viral protein, stable signal peptide (SSP), that does not undergo fusion itself but is required for the fusion process. However, the exact function of SSP in fusion is unknown. We aimed to understand the role of SSP in the fusion process by examining the structural changes that occur within SSP during the fusion process. We found that SSP undergoes two distinct structural changes; the first at pH 6 that is not associated with fusion, the second at below pH 5 that is associated with fusion activity. Furthermore, we found a mutation to a key residue of SSP, K33A, does not undergo these two structural changes; in fact, K33A is seen to undergo a different conformational change at pH 6. We believe this distinct conformation change is due to the loss of favorable interactions between the lysine at the end of the transmembrane helix of SSP. This disruption of favorable interaction then causes downstream effects to the SSP structure in the event of lowering pH. The difference in conformational changes between K33A and wildtype (WT) SSP is likely why K33A abrogates the fusion activity of GP2. We conclude that the conformational changes undergone by SSP are crucial for LASV fusion activity.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 拉沙病毒 (LASV) 是 沙粒病毒 家族的成员,利用低 pH 依赖性膜融合进入 宿主 细胞并引发感染。LASV是I类融合病毒,因此其融合蛋白GP2在功能上与其他I类融合蛋白相似,因为它遵循六螺旋束融合机制。LASV 融合的不典型之处在于它需要另一种病毒蛋白,即稳定信号肽(SSP),该蛋白本身不进行融合,但是融合过程所必需的。然而,SSP 在融合中的确切功能尚不清楚。我们的目的是通过检查融合过程中 SSP 内发生的结构变化来了解 SSP 在融合过程中的作用。我们发现 SSP 经历了两个不同的结构变化:第一个在 pH 6 时与融合无关,第二个在 pH 5 以下与融合活性相关。此外,我们发现 SSP K33A 的关键残基的 突变 不会经历这两个结构变化;事实上,K33A 在 pH 6 时经历了不同的构象变化。我们认为这种独特的构象变化是由于 SSP 跨膜螺旋末端的赖氨酸之间失去了有利的相互作用。如果 pH 值降低,这种有利相互作用的破坏就会对 SSP 结构产生下游影响。K33A 和野生型 (WT) SSP 之间构象变化的差异可能是 K33A 消除 GP2 融合活性的原因。我们得出的结论是,SSP 发生的构象变化对于 LASV 融合活性至关重要。

papers.title: Lymphocytic Choriomeningitis Virus Bearing GPC Mutations for Enhanced Tumor Tropism and Strong Anti-Tumor Activity
papers.abstract: The development of effective viroimmunotherapies for cancer relies on the ability of replicating viruses to infect the entire tumor tissue and induce comprehensive inflammation within the tumor microenvironment (TME). In this study, we investigate the impact of mutations in the glycoprotein (GP) of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) on tumor cell infectivity, replication, and the immune response. Specifically, we focus on two key positions in GP1 (181 and 185) that significantly enhance tumor cell infectivity and improve CD8+ T cell function in the GP-mutated LCMV strain LCMV P52. Our findings demonstrate that LCMV strain LCMV P52 replicates preferentially in vivo in tumors, exhibits improved tumor penetration, attracts functional CD8+ T cells more effectively to the tumor, and reprograms the tumor toward a more immunogenic microenvironment to allow for effective checkpoint inhibitor combination.

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究调查了GP 突变在LCMV中对肿瘤细胞感染性、复制能力和免疫应答的影响,重点关注LCMV P52株及其与肿瘤组织的相互作用。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究考察了LCMV P52株在体内的复制行为、其穿透肿瘤的能力以及其吸引功能性CD8+ T细胞进入肿瘤微环境的能力。
analysis_zh.main_results: 研究结果表明,LCMV P52 优先在肿瘤中复制,表现出改善的肿瘤渗透性,更有效地吸引功能性 CD8+ T 细胞,并将肿瘤微环境重新编程为更具免疫原性。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些结果解释为 LCMV 中的 GP 突变 可以增强其肿瘤趋向性和抗肿瘤活性的证据,为病毒免疫治疗提供了一种新方法。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以通过提高 LCMV 的肿瘤靶向能力来开发更有效的癌症病毒免疫疗法。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究为LCMV P52增强的肿瘤趋向性和抗肿瘤活性提供了有力的证据,但其研究结果仅限于体内观察,可能无法完全捕捉肿瘤微环境的复杂性。

papers.title: Metabolomics of in vivo inflammation identifies soluble sialic acid as a conserved myeloid-cell metabolite.
papers.abstract: During an immune response, metabolism changes dramatically. Metabolites are oxidized to power immune cell functions, serve as building blocks for proliferation, and act as effectors to regulate pathogen or host cells. Though metabolic changes in cultured cells have been studied extensively, metabolism changes in vivo are less understood. Here, we measured metabolomic changes across six mouse tissues in three models of immune activation: CpG-DNA cytokine storm, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection, and polyI:C viral mimetic injection; and carried out metabolomics in cultured macrophages activated with different stimuli. We found most metabolomic changes were exclusive to either inflamed tissues or cultured macrophages, although itaconate was strongly induced in both contexts. We then mechanistically dissected the role of the soluble sialic acid N-glycolylneuraminic acid, which is highly induced in inflamed tissues yet only modestly in cultured macrophages. This metabolite increases in tissues in different models of inflammation, and the analogous human metabolite, N-acetylneuraminic acid, rises in human patients experiencing inflammation. We found that N-glycolylneuraminic acid is produced in CD11b+ myeloid cells by cleavage of protein-bound sialic acid. However, blocking its production did not affect CpG-DNA liver inflammation or LCMV infection in mice. Therefore, these experiments identify soluble sialic acid as a conserved biomarker of inflammation in mice and humans and highlight the differences in metabolism between in vitro and in vivo models of inflammation.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores how metabolism changes during immune responses, focusing on identifying metabolites that could serve as biomarkers of inflammation. Using three models of immune activation in mice—CpG-DNA cytokine storm, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection, and polyI:C viral mimetic injection—the researchers measured metabolomic changes across six tissues and in cultured macrophages. They found that most metabolomic changes were specific to either inflamed tissues or cultured macrophages, with itaconate being a notable exception. However, blocking its production did not affect inflammation in mice, suggesting that its role may be more complex. The study highlights the differences in metabolism between in vitro and in vivo models of inflammation, offering potential insights for monitoring immune responses and guiding therapeutic strategies. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on models and the lack of direct functional validation.

papers.abstract_zh: 在 免疫应答 期间,新陈代谢发生巨大变化。代谢物被氧化以增强免疫细胞功能,作为增殖的基石,并作为调节病原体或 宿主 细胞的效应器。尽管培养细胞的代谢变化已被广泛研究,但体内代谢变化却知之甚少。在这里,我们测量了三种免疫激活模型中六种小鼠组织的代谢组变化:CpG-DNA细胞因子风暴、淋巴细胞脉络丛脑膜炎病毒感染和polyI:C病毒模拟注射;并在不同刺激激活的培养巨噬细胞中进行代谢组学。我们发现大多数代谢组变化只发生在发炎组织或培养的巨噬细胞中,尽管衣康酸在这两种情况下都被强烈诱导。然后,我们从机制上剖析了可溶性唾液酸 N-乙醇酰神经氨酸的作用,它在发炎组织中高度诱导,但在培养的巨噬细胞中仅适度诱导。这种代谢物在不同炎症模型的组织中增加,类似的人类代谢物 N-乙酰神经氨酸在经历炎症的人类患者中增加。我们发现 CD11b+ 骨髓细胞中通过蛋白质结合唾液酸的裂解产生 N-乙醇酰神经氨酸。然而,阻断其产生并不会影响小鼠的 CpG-DNA 肝脏炎症或 LCMV 感染。因此,这些实验将可溶性唾液酸确定为小鼠和人类炎症的保守生物标志物,并强调了体外和体内炎症模型之间代谢的差异。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查 免疫应答 期间新陈代谢如何变化,并确定可作为炎症生物标志物的代谢物。背景强调,虽然培养细胞的代谢变化已被充分了解,但体内的代谢变化仍然较少被研究。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用了三种小鼠免疫激活模型:CpG-DNA细胞因子风暴、淋巴细胞脉络丛脑膜炎病毒感染和polyI:C病毒模拟注射。它还包括用不同刺激激活的培养巨噬细胞的代谢组学分析。
analysis_zh.methods: 在三种免疫激活模型和培养的巨噬细胞中测量了六种小鼠组织的代谢组变化。该研究涉及分析体内和体外环境中的代谢物以比较它们的概况。
analysis_zh.main_results: 大多数代谢组学变化仅发生在发炎组织或培养的巨噬细胞中,尽管衣康酸在这两种情况下均被强烈诱导。研究发现,CD11b+ 骨髓细胞中通过蛋白质结合唾液酸的裂解产生 N-乙醇酰神经氨酸。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果确定可溶性唾液酸是小鼠和人类炎症的保守生物标志物,同时还强调了体外和体内炎症模型之间的代谢差异。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果提供了对炎症代谢特征的深入了解,这可以为监测 免疫应答 的生物标志物的开发提供信息,并有可能指导炎症性疾病的治疗策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据仅限于体内和体外模型,并且缺乏对 N-乙醇酰神经氨酸在炎症中的作用的直接功能验证,表明该结论的可信度中等。

papers.title: Temporal lymphatic tissue destruction and impairment of de novo T cell responses after an acute virus infection
papers.abstract: Abstract Post-acute infection sequelae (PAIS), which include diverse immunological alterations and clinical syndromes, represent a significant yet poorly understood phenomenon following acute viral infections. While the host typically resolves acute infections within weeks and develops virus-specific immunity, emerging evidence suggests that long-term symptoms can persist or arise after primary infection recovery. Using the acute lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection mouse model, we investigated potential mechanisms underlying immune-related PAIS. By combining mouse infections, different vaccine regimens, and immune monitoring with fluorescence microscopy and 3D image reconstruction of lymphatic tissues, we demonstrated that LCMV-recovered animals exhibit a prolonged immunocompromised state affecting dominantly de novo T cell responses. This is linked to the massive destruction of splenic lymphatic tissue, affecting the compartmentalization of the organ as well as crucial cell–cell contacts necessary for efficient T cell priming. Importantly, LCMV vaccination prevented LCMV-mediated lymphatic tissue destruction and the compromised immunological state. These findings underscore the importance of vaccination in preventing both acute virus infection-mediated pathology and potential PAIS. Our results highlight the complex interplay between virus infections, immune responses, and tissue integrity, challenging the common assumption that hosts fully recover their pre-infection homeostatic health state directly after an acute virus infection is controlled.

Global Health Protection Explore This Topic Search Search Clear Search Public Health What We Do Campaigns and Awareness Days Stories of Impact Resources View all search clear search Global Health Protection Menu clear search Public Health What We Do Campaigns and Awareness Days Stories of Impact Resources View All Home Related Topics Global Health What We Do Campaigns and Awareness Days Stories of Impact Resources View Menu World Field Epidemiology Day September 7, 2026 For Public Health Sept. 9, 2026, visit link for details. At a glance Some of the world's most dangerous disease outbreaks never make the headlines—and you may never hear about them at all. They don't close airports. They don't overwhelm hospitals. They don't disrupt daily life—or rattle the global economy. That's often because CDC and its global health security experts are on the frontlines—working with countries to quickly detect, respond to and contain outbreaks. This year, in recognition of World Field Epidemiology Day, the "Outbreaks You Never Heard About" campaign spotlights CDC-trained disease detectives and the crucial role they play in that work, strengthening the first line of defense against global health threats and helping protect American lives, livelihoods, and health security here at home. Outbreaks You Never Heard About: CDC Experts on the Frontlines View LargerDownload CDC's global health security experts are on the frontlines stopping deadly threats before they can spread in the U.S. In today's world, where a health threat overseas can reach U.S. communities in just 36 hours, stopping outbreaks at their source is one of the most effective ways we protect Americans at home and abroad. The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a stark reminder of how serious these threats can become when they spread undetected and gain ground. In the past two years alone, CDC's global health security experts helped contain more than 250 outbreaks across 40+ countries: from hemorrhagic fevers to dengue, and from Marburg to Guillain-Barré syndrome. These teams, based overseas and at CDC headquarters, form CDC's frontline global health security force. Together with partners across the U.S. government and around the globe, these world-class experts are on the frontlines keeping Americans safe. They not only lead emergency responses but also strengthen the systems that stop local disease outbreaks from becoming global crises, bolstering laboratories to quickly detect deadly pathogens, improving surveillance to track emerging threats, and training disease detectives to investigate and swiftly contain outbreaks. CDC-Trained Disease Detectives on the Frontlines At the center of many of these responses are CDC-trained field epidemiologists on the frontlines when dangerous outbreaks strike. These disease detectives are part of a global corps trained through CDC's landmark Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP). More than 25,000 disease detectives have been trained through CDC-supported FETPs since 1980 in more than 100 countries around the world, where they are positioned as a first line of defense against deadly disease threats. They are often the first on the ground when outbreaks happen—identifying threats, investigating cases in real time, tracking how diseases spread, identifying those at risk, and helping stop outbreaks before they escalate. Working at the very heart of outbreak response, these experts help stop dangerous outbreaks in their tracks and help keep them from ever reaching U.S. communities. Outbreaks You Never Heard About: Stories from the Frontlines Yet most of these outbreaks never make the news because they never escalate into global threats. And that's the point. These real-world examples with measurable results show how CDC's expertise helps move outbreaks from crisis to control before they reach U.S. communities, protecting Americans' health, safety, and livelihoods. How CDC Helped Stop a Deadly Virus Before It Spread View LargerDownload In 2025, CDC's global health security experts and Senegalese health officials rapidly contained a deadly outbreak of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, stopping it at the source before it could cross borders. In January 2025, a deadly virus surfaced in Senegal's Kaffrine Region. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever—a tick-borne disease that can also spread through infected animals and between humans—had sickened five people and killed one. With a high fatality rate and multiple pathways for transmission, even a small cluster can quickly become something much larger. Stopping the virus meant understanding not only who had become sick, but where they had been, who they had come into contact with, and whether the disease was also circulating among animals. CDC's Rapid Response Within hours, CDC's global health experts and Senegalese health officials sprang into action, activating Senegal's Emergency Operations Center and launching a coordinated response. Among those responding were CDC-trained disease detectives, working alongside veterinarians, doctors, and anthropologists to trace how the virus was moving between people, animals, and affected communities. Together, the teams identified and followed 51 potential contacts and tested more than 70 human and animal samples. They treated livestock, disinfected contaminated areas, and worked across human and animal health to identify possible exposures and interrupt transmission. It was the kind of response CDC's Field Epidemiology Training Program is designed to make possible: trained disease detectives already on the ground, able to move quickly when a dangerous threat emerges, and work across disciplines to stop it. Global Action. Local Impact. Thanks to these efforts, the outbreak was contained in just two weeks—with only five cases and no wider spread. The virus never moved beyond the affected area—protecting communities and livelihoods in Senegal and reducing the risk that a deadly outbreak could spread across borders cause significant human and economic harm and ultimately threaten Americans at home. Stopping Lassa Fever in Its Tracks View LargerDownload In 2024, when an American man returned to Iowa from Liberia unknowingly infected with Lassa fever, CDC experts acted fast to safeguard Americans from the threat, containing it before it could spread. In October 2024, an American man returned to Iowa after a trip to Liberia. Unknowingly, he carried Lassa fever, a potentially deadly virus found in parts of West Africa. In the days after his arrival, he developed symptoms and visited three healthcare facilities, using two ambulances and emergency services along the way. Despite efforts to treat him, tragically, he died. The case highlighted just how quickly a health threat overseas can become a threat here at home—and the critical role CDC's global health expertise plays in protecting communities around the world and in the United States. CDC's Rapid Response CDC's ability to respond in Iowa drew on 16 years of work in Liberia, where Lassa fever remains a persistent challenge. Working in partnership, CDC's global health teams and subject matter experts in Atlanta were able to provide Iowa health officials with the knowledge and guidance needed to diagnose the disease and prevent further spread. Over the years, CDC teams in Liberia have assessed health facilities, trained local staff, and worked with Liberia's Ministry of Health and the National Public Health Institute of Liberia to strengthen disease detection and response. CDC experts have conducted active case searches, strengthened case tracking and genetic sequencing, and trained frontline health workers to recognize and respond to diseases like Lassa fever. Those tools weren't just helping Liberia. When Lassa fever surfaced in Iowa, CDC's domestic and international teams mobilized quickly to support the state—providing laboratory confirmation, supporting the epidemiologic investigation and contact tracing, offering infection-prevention guidance, and helping protect healthcare workers who had been exposed. Global Action. Local Impact. Thanks to this rapid response, there was no additional spread in the United States beyond the single imported case. By strengthening the systems and expertise needed to confront diseases like Lassa fever where they occur, CDC is better prepared when those same threats reach U.S. shores—helping protect communities overseas and Americans here at home. Containing Ethiopia's First Marburg Outbreak Before It Spread View LargerDownload In 2025, global health experts, including CDC-trained disease detectives partnered with Ethiopian health officials to detect and contain Ethiopia's very first Marburg virus outbreak, before it could reach the United States. In November 2025, Ethiopia confronted a troubling historic episode: its first confirmed outbreak of Marburg virus. The deadly hemorrhagic fever quickly appeared across communities in the South Ethiopia and Sidama regions. By early December, 14 cases had been confirmed and nine people had died. With no previous Marburg outbreak experience to draw from, the challenge was immediate: find those at risk, interrupt transmission, and keep the virus from reaching more communities—or crossing Ethiopia's borders. CDC's Rapid Response From the earliest days of the outbreak, CDC experts worked alongside Ethiopia's Ministry of Health. At the center of that effort were 17 CDC-trained Ethiopian field epidemiologists who deployed into affected communities to investigate cases, trace contacts, and track the virus in real time. CDC experts and Ethiopian field epidemiologists strengthened laboratory testing and surveillance and reinforced infection prevention and control in health facilities. As new information came in, these teams used the data to guide the response—helping health officials see where the greatest risks remained and where action was needed most. CDC experts also looked beyond the immediate outbreak. They helped strengthen border health measures including in Addis Ababa international airport, a major hub with multiple flights to the United States. They advised on bat ecology to reduce the risk of future transmission from animals to people, and also worked with neighboring countries to assess their readiness should the virus spread farther. Global Action. Local Impact. Within one month, transmission was interrupted, and six weeks later, the outbreak was fully contained—with just 14 confirmed cases. Ultimately, the virus remained confined to two southern regions, never reached the capital, Addis Ababa, and never crossed an international border. As such, CDC's experts helped stop Ethiopia's first Marburg outbreak in its tracks before it could spread farther, threaten neighboring countries, or become a threat to the United States. Stopping an Unexplained Neurological Illness Outbreak View LargerDownload In 2023, CDC's global health security experts and country partners identified the source of a mystery neurological illness, Guillain-Barré syndrome, in Guatemala and quickly contained the spread before it could cross borders. In late 2023, a cluster of severe neurological illness began appearing along Guatemala's Pan-American Highway. Patients were rapidly developing Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a rare neurological disorder that can cause progressive muscle weakness and paralysis, potentially leading to respiratory failure. But GBS can be triggered by a range of infections and other conditions. As case numbers grew, health officials faced difficult questions: what was making people sick, and was the source still putting others at risk? With cases appearing along one of Central America's major travel and trade corridors linking the region to the U.S., finding the answer quickly mattered well beyond the affected communities. CDC's Rapid Response CDC country office experts worked alongside Field Epidemiology Training Program graduates, Guatemala's Ministries of Health and Agriculture, and regional partners to find the source. Teams searched door to door for additional cases, tested environmental samples, and compared those who became sick with those who did not to identify possible risk factors. Two CDC Epidemic Intelligence Service officers were deployed to strengthen the investigation and help determine what the cases had in common. The laboratory offered another critical clue. Using advanced genomic sequencing to analyze patient and environmental samples, investigators detected Campylobacter, a common foodborne bacterium. Combined with epidemiologic findings linking illness to uncooked or poorly cooked foods, the evidence pointed to this foodborne bacterial contamination as the likely trigger. Together, the field investigation and laboratory evidence gave health officials what they needed to understand the outbreak—and act. Global Action. Local Impact. Thanks to the rapid investigation, within 30 days, health officials had identified the likely cause, and within 90 days, the outbreak was contained. In all, 87 cases were identified, but the outbreak remained localized with no cross-border spread. By finding the likely trigger and stopping the outbreak quickly, CDC and country partners protected communities while reducing the risk that an unexplained health threat along a major travel and trade corridor could spread farther—including toward the United States. Finding Deadly Diseases Hidden in Plain Sight View LargerDownload In Nigeria, a CDC-trained disease detective used innovative post-mortem surveillance to uncover hidden Lassa fever and dengue cases—helping stop threats before they could spread farther and put Americans at risk. In northwest Nigeria, people were dying with fever, but the disease that killed them was not always known. Lassa fever and dengue can look like other common illnesses in their early stages, allowing dangerous infections to go undetected. For health officials, those missed diagnoses created a troubling blind spot. When someone died without a clear diagnosis, an important warning could disappear from the surveillance system even while the disease continued circulating in the community. In Sokoto State, a CDC-trained disease detective recognized the gap. CDC's Rapid Response Instead of waiting for the next diagnosed case to reveal what was circulating, the disease detective helped establish a new post-mortem surveillance system at two referral hospitals. Teams interviewed family members and caregivers, reviewed medical records, andintroduced post-mortem testing for Lassa fever, dengue, and malariausing blood samples from people who had died following a fever. The approach gave health officials another way to look beneath the surface to identify dangerous infections that routine surveillance might never see, and better understand what diseases were circulating in the community. Global Action. Local Impact. The results revealed what traditional surveillance had missed. Using this novel approach, investigators uncovered 11 Lassa fever infections and one dengue infection that had previously gone unrecognized. By bringing hidden threats into view, a CDC-trained disease detective gave local health officials the critical information they needed to identify dangerous diseases and guide public health action, ultimately reducing the risk that an undetected threat could eventually reach the United States. Why It Matters: Outbreaks You Never Heard About—Because CDC Was There Behind many of the outbreaks you never hear about are CDC global health experts and CDC-trained disease detectives on the frontlines containing dangerous health threats around the world. They are often among the first on the ground when outbreaks strike: finding cases, tracing contacts, tracking how diseases spread, identifying hidden threats, and helping stop them before they can escalate. That impact reaches across the globe. Since 1980, CDC's landmark Field Epidemiology Training Program has trained more than 25,000 disease detectives in more than 100 countries, building a global corps equipped to detect threats early, investigate outbreaks in real time, and act quickly when every hour counts. That reach translates into real-world impact. Marburg was stopped before it crossed Ethiopia's borders. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever was contained in Senegal in just two weeks. Disease detectives in Nigeria uncovered deadly infections that had been circulating undetected. And when Lassa fever reached Iowa, the virus was stopped in its tracks—with no additional spread. Through global health security, CDC is helping countries detect outbreaks earlier, respond faster, and contain dangerous diseases at their source—before they can threaten U.S. communities, disrupt travel and trade, or put American lives and livelihoods at risk. Stopping outbreaks before they spread isn't just smart public health. It's national security. It's economic security. And it's what CDC's global health experts and CDC-trained disease detectives do every day to help keep Americans safe. Over the years, CDC teams in Liberia have assessed health facilities, trained local staff, and worked with Liberia's Ministry of Health and the National Public Health Institute of Liberia to strengthen disease detection and response. CDC experts have conducted active case searches, strengthened case tracking and genetic sequencing, and trained frontline health workers to recognize and respond to diseases like Lassa fever. Those tools weren't just helping Liberia. When Lassa fever surfaced in Iowa, CDC's domestic and international teams mobilized quickly to support the state—providing laboratory confirmation, supporting the epidemiologic investigation and contact tracing, offering infection-prevention guidance, and helping protect healthcare workers who had been exposed. Global Action. Local Impact. Thanks to this rapid response, there was no additional spread in the United States beyond the single imported case. By strengthening the systems and expertise needed to confront diseases like Lassa fever where they occur, CDC is better prepared when those same threats reach U.S. shores—helping protect communities overseas and Americans here at home. Containing Ethiopia's First Marburg Outbreak Before It Spread View LargerDownload In 2025, global health experts, including CDC-trained disease detectives partnered with Ethiopian health officials to detect and contain Ethiopia's very first Marburg virus outbreak, before it could reach the United States. In November 2025, Ethiopia confronted a troubling historic episode: its first confirmed outbreak of Marburg virus. The deadly hemorrhagic fever quickly appeared across communities in the South Ethiopia and Sidama regions. By early December, 14 cases had been confirmed and nine people had died. With no previous Marburg outbreak experience to draw from, the challenge was immediate: find those at risk, interrupt transmission, and keep the virus from reaching more communities—or crossing Ethiopia's borders. CDC's Rapid Response From the earliest days of the outbreak, CDC experts worked alongside Ethiopia's Ministry of Health. At the center of that effort were 17 CDC-trained Ethiopian field epidemiologists who deployed into affected communities to investigate cases, trace contacts, and track the virus in real time. CDC experts and Ethiopian field epidemiologists strengthened laboratory testing and surveillance and reinforced infection prevention and control in health facilities. As new information came in, these teams used the data to guide the response—helping health officials see where the greatest risks remained and where action was needed most. CDC experts also looked beyond the immediate outbreak. They helped strengthen border health measures including in Addis Ababa international airport, a major hub with multiple flights to the United States. They advised on bat ecology to reduce the risk of future transmission from animals to people, and also worked with neighboring countries to assess their readiness should the virus spread farther. Global Action. Local Impact. Within one month, transmission was interrupted, and six weeks later, the outbreak was fully contained—with just 14 confirmed cases. Ultimately, the virus remained confined to two southern regions, never reached the capital, Addis Ababa, and never crossed an international border. As such, CDC's experts helped stop Ethiopia's first Marburg outbreak in its tracks before it could spread farther, threaten neighboring countries, or become a threat to the United States. Stopping an Unexplained Neurological Illness Outbreak View LargerDownload In 2023, CDC's global health security experts and country partners identified the source of a mystery neurological illness, Guillain-Barré syndrome, in Guatemala and quickly contained the spread before it could cross borders. In late 2023, a cluster of severe neurological illness began appearing along Guatemala's Pan-American Highway. Patients were rapidly developing Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a rare neurological disorder that can cause progressive muscle weakness and paralysis, potentially leading to respiratory failure. But GBS can be triggered by a range of infections and other conditions. As case numbers grew, health officials faced difficult questions: what was making people sick, and was the source still putting others at risk? With cases appearing along one of Central America's major travel and trade corridors linking the region to the U.S., finding the answer quickly mattered well beyond the affected communities. CDC's Rapid Response CDC country office experts worked alongside Field Epidemiology Training Program graduates, Guatemala's Ministries of Health and Agriculture, and regional partners to find the source. Teams searched door to door for additional cases, tested environmental samples, and compared those who became sick with those who did not to identify possible risk factors. Two CDC Epidemic Intelligence Service officers were deployed to strengthen the investigation and help determine what the cases had in common. The laboratory offered another critical clue. Using advanced genomic sequencing to analyze patient and environmental samples, investigators detected Campylobacter, a common foodborne bacterium. Combined with epidemiologic findings linking illness to uncooked or poorly cooked foods, the evidence pointed to this foodborne bacterial contamination as the likely trigger. Together, the field investigation and laboratory evidence gave health officials what they needed to understand the outbreak—and act. Global Action. Local Impact. Thanks to the rapid investigation, within 30 days, health officials had identified the likely cause, and within 90 days, the outbreak was contained. In all, 87 cases were identified, but the outbreak remained localized with no cross-border spread. By finding the likely trigger and stopping the outbreak quickly, CDC and country partners protected communities while reducing the risk that an unexplained health threat along a major travel and trade corridor could spread farther—including toward the United States. Finding Deadly Diseases Hidden in Plain Sight View LargerDownload In Nigeria, a CDC-trained disease detective used innovative post-mortem surveillance to uncover hidden Lassa fever and dengue cases—helping stop threats before they could spread farther and put Americans at risk. In northwest Nigeria, people were dying with fever, but the disease that killed them was not always known. Lassa fever and dengue can look like other common illnesses in their early stages, allowing dangerous infections to go undetected. For health officials, those missed diagnoses created a troubling blind spot. When someone died without a clear diagnosis, an important warning could disappear from the surveillance system even while the disease continued circulating in the community. In Sokoto State, a CDC-trained disease detective recognized the gap. CDC's Rapid Response Instead of waiting for the next diagnosed case to reveal what was circulating, the disease detective helped establish a new post-mortem surveillance system at two referral hospitals. Teams interviewed family members and caregivers, reviewed medical records, andintroduced post-mortem testing for Lassa fever, dengue, and malariausing blood samples from people who had died following a fever. The approach gave health officials another way to look beneath the surface to identify dangerous infections that routine surveillance might never see, and better understand what diseases were circulating in the community. Global Action. Local Impact. The results revealed what traditional surveillance had missed. Using this novel approach, investigators uncovered 11 Lassa fever infections and one dengue infection that had previously gone unrecognized. By bringing hidden threats into view, a CDC-trained disease detective gave local health officials the critical information they needed to identify dangerous diseases and guide public health action, ultimately reducing the risk that an undetected threat could eventually reach the United States. Why It Matters: Outbreaks You Never Heard About—Because CDC Was There Behind many of the outbreaks you never hear about are CDC global health experts and CDC-trained disease detectives on the frontlines containing dangerous health threats around the world. They are often among the first on the ground when outbreaks strike: finding cases, tracing contacts, tracking how diseases spread, identifying hidden threats, and helping stop them before they can escalate. That impact reaches across the globe. Since 1980, CDC's landmark Field Epidemiology Training Program has trained more than 25,000 disease detectives in more than 100 countries, building a global corps equipped to detect threats early, investigate outbreaks in real time, and act quickly when every hour counts. That reach translates into real-world impact. Marburg was stopped before it crossed Ethiopia's borders. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever was contained in Senegal in just two weeks. Disease detectives in Nigeria uncovered deadly infections that had been circulating undetected. And when Lassa fever reached Iowa, the virus was stopped in its tracks—with no additional spread. Through global health security, CDC is helping countries detect outbreaks earlier, respond faster, and contain dangerous diseases at their source—before they can threaten U.S. communities, disrupt travel and trade, or put American lives and livelihoods at risk. Stopping outbreaks before they spread isn't just smart public health. It's national security. It's economic security. And it's what CDC's global health experts and CDC-trained disease detectives do every day to help keep Americans safe. Pick countries on the world map and get breaking news alerts in your browser — free, no app.Turn on alerts →× Latest News Breaking News Headlines Stories Videos Become a Publisher News Search Nigeria About Us Contact Us Search 🔔 Head Topics Nigeria Latest News Breaking News Headlines Stories Videos Become a Publisher Oyo reports 131 suspected Lassa fever cases, 6 confirmed, 1 death 📆 10/09/2026 20:50:00 News News Lassa Fever, Oyo State, Nigeria 📆10/09/2026 20:50:00 📰Source: PremiumTimesng ⏱211 sec. here / 13 min. at publisher 📊News: 97% · Publisher: 78% Oyo State has reported 131 suspected Lassa fever cases, with 6 confirmed cases and 1 death since January 2026. The state's health commissioner has urged residents to maintain a high index of suspicion and practice good environmental hygiene. A hospital bed space in Nigeria Oyo State Government has raised the alarm over the spread of Lassa fever , urging healthcare workers to treat every patient as potentially infectious, as the state recorded five confirmed cases and one death. Dr Oluwaserimi Ajetunmobi, the state's Commissioner for Health, gave the directive while outlining the state's preparedness and response measures against Lassa fever and other viral haemorrhagic fevers. Ajetunmobi said the state had recorded 131 suspected Lassa fever cases between January and September 8, 2026, adding that the disease remained endemic in some parts of the state. Advertisement The state had recorded 131 suspected Lassa fever cases between January and September 8, 2026, adding that the disease remained endemic in some parts of the state. She said that suspected cases were now being detected beyond the period traditionally associated with outbreaks. According to her, although Lassa fever cases were usually more common between October or November and March or April, the state continued to record suspected cases during the rainy season. The commissioner, however, attributed the continued risk partly to poor environmental hygiene and the presence of multimammate rats, urging residents to dispose of waste properly, seal openings in their homes and keep food securely covered. She, therefore, urged residents experiencing persistent fever, headache, sore throat, vomiting or other unusual symptoms to seek medical attention promptly and disclose relevant travel history, saying that the state had activated its Public Health Emergency Operations Centre to strengthen coordination and preparedness for outbreak of infectious diseases. Meanwhile, five confirmed cases of diphtheria with two deaths have been recorded in the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCT) out of 15 suspected cases investigated in the territory. Consequently, the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) has deployed surveillance and vaccination teams to priority settlements in Karshi where the reported cases were recorded and surrounding communities. Mandate Secretary, Health Services and Environment Secretariat, FCTA, Dr Adedolapo Fasawe, who disclosed this yesterday during an advocacy campaign and community engagement on the prevention and control of diphtheria at the Emir of Karshi's Palace in the Abuja Municipal Area Council, stated that the teams, working with supervisors and others, are conducting case searches, assessing vaccination gaps and identifying children who have missed their routine vaccinations. Fasawe noted that the vaccination efforts will prioritise zero-dose and under-immunised children, adding that the administration is moving beyond responding to individual cases to strengthening protection across the entire FCT. Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic fever caused by the Lassa virus. Symptoms of Lassa fever can include fever, sore throat, vomiting, weakness, and bleeding from body openings. Lassa fever is traditionally associated with the dry season, particularly around October and November, and again around March and April. However, the state has recorded suspected cases outside these periods, which may be attributed to poor environmental hygiene and the presence of multimammate rats. Residents are advised to practice good environmental hygiene by keeping their environments clean, properly disposing of refuse, covering openings through which rodents could enter homes, and ensuring that food is kept covered. They should also wash their hands regularly with soap and water or use hand sanitiser where necessary. Healthcare workers are urged to observe appropriate infection prevention and control measures when attending to patients presenting with fever or other symptoms. Symptoms that should raise suspicion include fever, sore throat, vomiting, weakness, and, in severe cases, bleeding from body openings. Residents are advised not to conceal illness or delay seeking medical attention, as late presentation could result in complications. Centre Expansion 8 days ago Home Health Oyo Raises Alarm Over Lassa Fever as FCT Records Diphtheria Deaths BrandIconImage about 18 hours ago Five Lassa fever cases, one death recorded in Oyo; FCT deploys vaccination teams after diphtheria outbreak claims two lives. The Oyo State Government has raised concerns over the continued spread of Lassa fever after recording five confirmed cases and one death, warning healthcare workers to maintain a high level of caution when attending to patients with symptoms associated with the disease. The state’s Commissioner for Health, Dr Oluwaserimi Ajetunmobi, gave the warning while outlining measures being implemented by the government to strengthen surveillance, preparedness and response to Lassa fever and other viral haemorrhagic fevers. Ajetunmobi disclosed that the state had recorded 131 suspected cases of Lassa fever between January and September 8, 2026. She noted that the disease remained endemic in some parts of Oyo, making sustained surveillance and public awareness essential to preventing further transmission. According to the commissioner, health authorities are becoming increasingly concerned that suspected cases are being detected outside the period traditionally associated with heightened Lassa fever transmission. Lassa fever typically records higher incidence between October or November and March or April. However, Ajetunmobi said Oyo had continued to record suspected infections during the rainy season, indicating that the risk of transmission was no longer confined strictly to the conventional peak period. She linked part of the continuing risk to poor environmental sanitation and exposure to multimammate rats, which are recognised as the primary reservoir of the Lassa fever virus. The commissioner consequently urged residents to take greater responsibility for maintaining clean surroundings, disposing of refuse properly, sealing openings through which rodents could enter homes and ensuring that food is adequately covered and protected from contamination. She also advised residents who develop persistent fever, headache, sore throat, vomiting or other unusual symptoms to seek medical attention without delay. Residents were further encouraged to provide accurate travel histories to healthcare professionals, particularly where such information could assist in determining possible exposure to infectious diseases. Ajetunmobi said the state had activated its Public Health Emergency Operations Centre as part of efforts to improve coordination, surveillance and preparedness for outbreaks of infectious diseases. She also directed healthcare workers to approach suspected cases with appropriate caution and infection-prevention measures, stressing the need for early detection and prompt management to reduce the risk of further transmission. FCT records two deaths from diphtheria Meanwhile, the Federal Capital Territory Administration has recorded five confirmed cases of diphtheria and two deaths out of 15 suspected cases investigated in the territory. The development has prompted the administration to intensify surveillance and vaccination activities in affected communities, particularly in Karshi, where the reported cases were identified. Vaccination and surveillance teams have been deployed to priority settlements in Karshi and surrounding communities as health authorities seek to identify additional cases, close immunisation gaps and prevent further spread of the potentially fatal bacterial disease. The Mandate Secretary of the Health Services and Environment Secretariat, Federal Capital Territory Administration, Dr Adedolapo Fasawe, disclosed the figures yesterday during an advocacy campaign and community engagement on diphtheria prevention and control at the palace of the Emir of Karshi in the Abuja Municipal Area Council. Fasawe said the teams were conducting active case searches while also assessing vaccination gaps and identifying children who had missed their routine immunisations. She explained that the intervention was designed not merely to respond to confirmed infections but also to strengthen community-wide protection against further transmission. The vaccination exercise will particularly target zero-dose children — those who have never received routine vaccines — as well as under-immunised children who have received some but not all recommended doses. Fasawe said the FCT administration was broadening its approach from responding to individual cases to strengthening preventive measures across communities. The simultaneous health alerts in Oyo and the FCT highlight the continuing importance of disease surveillance, vaccination, environmental hygiene and early medical intervention in preventing infectious disease outbreaks. Health authorities are urging residents not to ignore persistent or unusual symptoms and are encouraging communities to cooperate with surveillance and vaccination teams as public health officials work to contain the threats. The state government, through its Commissioner for Health, Dr Oluwaserimi Ajetunmobi, has warned healthcare workers to exercise caution and is implementing measures to enhance surveillance and response efforts. Additionally, a diphtheria outbreak has claimed two lives, prompting further action. The administration has intensified vaccination and monitoring activities in the affected Karshi community. While the exact source of the Lassa fever cases is not specified, the government is actively working to mitigate the risk of further transmission. The situation remains under investigation, with no confirmed details on the origin or containment strategies beyond the stated measures.

news.content: Skip to main content Global editionSaturday, September 12, 2026 Streamline Search⌘KWriteSign inJoin Streamline StreamlineGlobal edition LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSportDirectoryHouse HuntingPeopleHistoryMore LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSport Back to News/Health Health NCDC Warns of Lassa Fever Surge Ahead of Dry Season, Highlights Critical Health System Gaps The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control has urged early preparation ahead of the November-April Lassa fever peak, warning of functional healthcare capacity gaps. Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Sep 10, 2026Updated Sep 10, 20264 min read Report article Follow on Google News Try askingWhy does this matter? Advertisement from Treadville Coffee Kenya . The first 10 seconds cannot be skipped. Ad playing Ad playing. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has issued a nationwide alert ahead of the impending dry season, warning that the country faces a critical window to upgrade its Lassa fever preparedness before viral transmission peaks. During a press briefing in Abuja on Wednesday, NCDC Director-General Dr Jide Idris highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the national health architecture. An after-action review of the 2026 outbreak revealed severe disparities between theoretical healthcare capacity and functional reality on the ground, leaving both patients and healthcare workers at significant risk as the November to April peak season approaches. The agency warned that state governments and communities must initiate preventive actions immediately, rather than waiting for infection figures to climb, to avoid the high mortality rates that have historically characterised the outbreak period. The Approaching Seasonal Peak While Lassa fever infections occur throughout the year in Nigeria, the disease exhibits a pronounced seasonal spike during the dry season. The period from November to April typically sees a dramatic increase in cases, driven by environmental factors and human-rodent interactions as food sources change. Dr Idris emphasised that the current pre-peak period offers a vital opportunity for intervention. “We are not yet in that peak period, and that gives us an important opportunity to act now,” he told journalists. The agency’s strategy focuses on mobilising households, healthcare facilities, and state governments to implement preventive measures before the health system becomes overwhelmed. To coordinate the response, the NCDC has developed an Accelerated Readiness Plan. The framework prioritises earlier detection, faster laboratory testing, improved patient referral systems, and stronger infection prevention and control (IPC) protocols across regional health centres. The Illusion of Healthcare Capacity A central and troubling finding from the NCDC’s after-action review of the early 2026 response was the dangerous gap between the healthcare capacity that exists on paper and what is genuinely functional during a crisis. Dr Idris cited the availability of specialised medical equipment as a primary example of this disparity. “For example, having a dialysis machine does not mean dialysis is available if the trained personnel, consumables, water treatment, maintenance, and other requirements needed to operate it are not in place,” he explained. This lack of functional readiness has repeatedly compromised patient care when treatment centres receive sudden influxes of severe Lassa fever cases. The NCDC has urged state ministries of health to audit their actual operational capacities rather than relying on hardware inventories that do not reflect clinical readiness. High-Burden States and Resource Reliance The burden of Lassa fever is not distributed evenly across the country. According to NCDC data, five states currently account for 86 percent of all reported cases in 2026: Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo, and Benue. Despite this concentrated and recurring risk, the agency noted a concerning lack of local ownership in outbreak preparedness. The review identified that many state and local governments remain overly dependent on federal resources, often delaying vital preparatory activities while waiting for national intervention. Dr Idris called out the delays in releasing budgeted funds at the sub-national level, stressing that state governments must take proactive financial and operational responsibility for their jurisdictions. Environmental sanitation and community waste management, which are critical to rodent control, fall squarely within the remit of local authorities. Challenges in Care and Worker Safety The 2026 review also highlighted behavioral and systemic challenges that continue to drive up the case fatality rate. Chief among these is the late presentation of patients to appropriate medical facilities. Many individuals engage in self-medication or visit multiple primary healthcare providers before Lassa fever is suspected. Because early symptoms frequently mimic malaria, this delays the administration of Ribavirin, the specific antiviral drug used to treat the disease. This delay significantly reduces the chances of patient survival and increases the window for onward transmission within communities. Furthermore, the late diagnosis places immense pressure on frontline medical staff. The NCDC reported continued infections among healthcare workers, particularly when facilities operate under strain. The agency has reiterated the necessity of assuming Lassa fever as a possibility in endemic areas, urging clinical staff to adopt protective measures from their very first contact with a symptomatic patient, rather than waiting for laboratory confirmation. Environmental Risks and the One Health Approach At the household level, persistent environmental risks remain the primary driver of the zoonotic disease, which is transmitted through the urine and faeces of the multimammate rat. The NCDC warned against unsafe food storage practices, such as drying grain on bare ground or leaving food uncovered in areas accessible to rodents. Households are advised to store staples like rice, garri, beans, and maize in tightly sealed containers and to block structural openings that allow rats into homes. Recognising that the health sector alone cannot defeat the virus, the NCDC is actively promoting a “One Health” approach. This strategy requires coordinated action across the health, environment, agriculture, and livestock sectors. Local governments have been tasked with improving community waste disposal to eliminate the refuse dumps that attract rodent populations close to human habitation. Closing the Readiness Gap As the country moves closer to November, the NCDC is distributing essential response commodities, including personal protective equipment (PPE), hygiene materials, and Ribavirin, to designated treatment centres. Additional training in clinical case management is being rolled out for healthcare workers in the highest-burden states. However, the agency insists that clinical readiness must be matched by community vigilance and robust state-level funding. How did this story land? No sign-in required. Choose up to two. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has issued a nationwide alert ahead of the impending dry season, warning that the country faces a critical window to upgrade its Lassa fever preparedness before viral transmission peaks. During a press briefing in Abuja on Wednesday, NCDC Director-General Dr Jide Idris highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the national health architecture. An after-action review of the 2026 outbreak revealed severe disparities between theoretical healthcare capacity and functional reality on the ground, leaving both patients and healthcare workers at significant risk as the November to April peak season approaches. The agency warned that state governments and communities must initiate preventive actions immediately, rather than waiting for infection figures to climb, to avoid the high mortality rates that have historically characterised the outbreak period. The Approaching Seasonal Peak While Lassa fever infections occur throughout the year in Nigeria, the disease exhibits a pronounced seasonal spike during the dry season. The period from November to April typically sees a dramatic increase in cases, driven by environmental factors and human-rodent interactions as food sources change. Dr Idris emphasised that the current pre-peak period offers a vital opportunity for intervention. “We are not yet in that peak period, and that gives us an important opportunity to act now,” he told journalists. The agency’s strategy focuses on mobilising households, healthcare facilities, and state governments to implement preventive measures before the health system becomes overwhelmed. To coordinate the response, the NCDC has developed an Accelerated Readiness Plan. The framework prioritises earlier detection, faster laboratory testing, improved patient referral systems, and stronger infection prevention and control (IPC) protocols across regional health centres. The Illusion of Healthcare Capacity A central and troubling finding from the NCDC’s after-action review of the early 2026 response was the dangerous gap between the healthcare capacity that exists on paper and what is genuinely functional during a crisis. Dr Idris cited the availability of specialised medical equipment as a primary example of this disparity. “For example, having a dialysis machine does not mean dialysis is available if the trained personnel, consumables, water treatment, maintenance, and other requirements needed to operate it are not in place,” he explained. This lack of functional readiness has repeatedly compromised patient care when treatment centres receive sudden influxes of severe Lassa fever cases. The NCDC has urged state ministries of health to audit their actual operational capacities rather than relying on hardware inventories that do not reflect clinical readiness. High-Burden States and Resource Reliance The burden of Lassa fever is not distributed evenly across the country. According to NCDC data, five states currently account for 86 percent of all reported cases in 2026: Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo, and Benue. Despite this concentrated and recurring risk, the agency noted a concerning lack of local ownership in outbreak preparedness. The review identified that many state and local governments remain overly dependent on federal resources, often delaying vital preparatory activities while waiting for national intervention. Dr Idris called out the delays in releasing budgeted funds at the sub-national level, stressing that state governments must take proactive financial and operational responsibility for their jurisdictions. Environmental sanitation and community waste management, which are critical to rodent control, fall squarely within the remit of local authorities. Challenges in Care and Worker Safety The 2026 review also highlighted behavioral and systemic challenges that continue to drive up the case fatality rate. Chief among these is the late presentation of patients to appropriate medical facilities. Many individuals engage in self-medication or visit multiple primary healthcare providers before Lassa fever is suspected. Because early symptoms frequently mimic malaria, this delays the administration of Ribavirin, the specific antiviral drug used to treat the disease. This delay significantly reduces the chances of patient survival and increases the window for onward transmission within communities. Furthermore, the late diagnosis places immense pressure on frontline medical staff. The NCDC reported continued infections among healthcare workers, particularly when facilities operate under strain. The agency has reiterated the necessity of assuming Lassa fever as a possibility in endemic areas, urging clinical staff to adopt protective measures from their very first contact with a symptomatic patient, rather than waiting for laboratory confirmation. Environmental Risks and the One Health Approach At the household level, persistent environmental risks remain the primary driver of the zoonotic disease, which is transmitted through the urine and faeces of the multimammate rat. The NCDC warned against unsafe food storage practices, such as drying grain on bare ground or leaving food uncovered in areas accessible to rodents. Households are advised to store staples like rice, garri, beans, and maize in tightly sealed containers and to block structural openings that allow rats into homes. Recognising that the health sector alone cannot defeat the virus, the NCDC is actively promoting a “One Health” approach. This strategy requires coordinated action across the health, environment, agriculture, and livestock sectors. Local governments have been tasked with improving community waste disposal to eliminate the refuse dumps that attract rodent populations close to human habitation. Closing the Readiness Gap As the country moves closer to November, the NCDC is distributing essential response commodities, including personal protective equipment (PPE), hygiene materials, and Ribavirin, to designated treatment centres. Additional training in clinical case management is being rolled out for healthcare workers in the highest-burden states. However, the agency insists that clinical readiness must be matched by community vigilance and robust state-level funding. How did this story land? No sign-in required. Choose up to two. analysis.time: The NCDC issued the advisory ahead of the November-to-April Lassa fever peak season, with the press briefing held on September 9, 2026. The publication date of the news report is September 10, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The advisory is directed at households and communities across Nigeria, with a focus on high-risk areas where the agency will intensify its 'Turn a Community Orange' approach.
analysis.event: The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) urged Nigerians to take preventive measures such as storing food safely and blocking rodent entry points to mitigate Lassa fever transmission ahead of the peak season. This is a confirmed public health advisory, not an outbreak report.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The 2026 After-Action Review identified several risks, including delayed care-seeking, prolonged self-treatment for suspected malaria, continued infections among healthcare workers, poor sanitation, unsafe food storage, and persistent rodent exposure. These factors contribute to the potential spread of Lassa fever and strain on health systems.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The NCDC has outlined an Accelerated Readiness Plan, which includes early detection, rapid investigation, laboratory testing, infection prevention, and availability of medicines and protective equipment. The plan is under implementation, and the response is ongoing with commitments from environment, livestock, and agriculture ministries.

analysis.brief_en: The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has issued an advisory urging Nigerians to take preventive measures against Lassa fever ahead of its peak season, which typically runs from November to April. The advisory emphasizes the importance of storing food in covered containers, maintaining cleanliness, and blocking rodent entry points to reduce the risk of transmission. This recommendation follows a national health security press briefing held on September 9, 2026, in Abuja, where the director-general, Dr Jide Idris, highlighted the need for preparedness before the health system faces increased pressure. The 2026 After-Action Review identified several challenges, including delayed care-seeking, prolonged self-treatment for suspected malaria, and persistent rodent exposure, which contribute to the spread of the disease. The NCDC's Accelerated Readiness Plan focuses on early detection, rapid investigation, and infection prevention, with additional resources allocated to high-risk areas. The plan also incorporates a 'Turn a Community Orange' approach to drive preventive behavior and early reporting, under a One Health framework that involves collaboration across health, environment, agriculture, livestock, and local government sectors. Idris urged states to fund preparedness efforts before cases rise, emphasizing the gap between theoretical capacity and functional readiness in healthcare systems.

news.content_zh: 尼日利亚疾病控制和预防中心 (NCDC) 已发布建议,敦促尼日利亚人在 拉沙热 高峰季节(通常为 11 月至 4 月)之前采取预防措施。该建议强调了将食物储存在有盖容器中、保持清洁和堵塞啮齿动物进入点以降低 传播 风险的重要性。这项建议是在 2026 年 9 月 9 日在阿布贾举行的国家卫生安全新闻发布会上提出的,会上总干事吉德·伊德里斯博士强调了在卫生系统面临更大压力之前做好准备的必要性。2026 年行动后审查确定了一些挑战,包括延迟就医、因疑似疟疾而延长自我 治疗 以及持续接触啮齿动物,这些都导致了疾病的传播。NCDC 的加速准备计划侧重于早期发现、快速调查和感染预防,并向高风险地区分配额外资源。该计划还纳入了“变成社区橙色”的方法,以推动预防行为和早期报告,在一个健康框架下,涉及健康、环境、农业、畜牧业和地方政府部门之间的合作。伊德里斯敦促各州在病例增加之前为准备工作提供资金,并强调医疗保健系统的理论能力和功能准备之间的差距。

Special Reports > Features HHS Hires Vax Skeptic for Deaths Investigation; Fauci Opens Up; China's Cancer Tx — A weekly roundup of healthcare investigations by Rachael Robertson, Enterprise & Investigative Writer, MedPage Today September 9, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. recently hired Lt. Col. Theresa Long, MD, MPHopens in a new tab or window, who has no training in vaccines or viruses, to investigate unsubstantiated claims about service members dying after being vaccinated against COVID. Long has a history of questioning the safety of COVID vaccines and parroting Kennedy's view that vaccines may cause autism. She's even testified that she knows of 28 service members who died as a result of the vaccines and many more who lost pregnancies. (New York Times) Anthony Fauci, MD, recently sat down with Georgetown University colleague Lawrence Gostin, JD, a global health policy expert, for a 2-hour interviewopens in a new tab or window. Fauci defended early responses to the COVID pandemic, rejected claims that mRNA COVID vaccines are unsafe, and criticized global aid cuts, while discussing other hot-button issues. (Science) Bob Garry, PhD, a renowned expert on dangerous viruses, has been a key voice in pushing back against COVID lab leak proponents. In March 2020, he published a paper after analyzing SARS-CoV-2 and wrote that the virus was not lab-created but likely traced to bats. Now, Garry's life's work, like developing a treatment for Lassa fever, is at risk due to Trump administration funding cutsopens in a new tab or window. Garry can't take on any doctoral students because he can't guarantee funding for their work. (Bloomberg) Before holding political office, Sen. Roger Marshall, MDopens in a new tab or window (R-Kan.), sued more than 700 patients over outstanding medical bills while he was practicing as an ob/gyn. A whopping 81 of these patients were arrested for missing court dates. Many lived in a rural county with high poverty rates and some of the unpaid bills were as little as $101. These patients faced steep 18% annual interest rates and had their bank accounts garnished. Marshall is seeking reelection this fall. (New York Times) CAR-T therapy can be a lifeline for people with certain cancers, but it also can be prohibitively expensive. While the treatment was pioneered in the U.S., China has surged aheadopens in a new tab or window as a leader in CAR-T therapy and as a haven for some patients from rich countries who pay about half as much as they would in the U.S., India, or Australia. It also offers CAR-T treatment for indications not yet approved in the U.S., such as stomach cancer. For instance, in a letter to the state's attorney general, they said they paid thousands of dollars to complete the program but never received a diploma or transcript. It wasn't shuttered until years later when FBI's Operation Nightingale took it down. A 2009 Florida law loosened nursing school regulations, which contributed to a proliferation of bad actors and made it harder for the state to close them. (Orlando Sentinel) Marijuana regulators in Colorado have a history of lagging behind in warning consumers about known concerns about products. For example, it took them nearly 15 months to warn the public about 1906 Midnight Drops, a popular marijuana-based sleep aidopens in a new tab or window, after reports of liver damage tied to the product surfaced. Meanwhile, the manufacturer had halted production. A ProPublica and Denver Gazette analysis found that regulators took an average of 7 months to warn the public after receiving a complaint.
